sections.content: ARTICLE 28 ACADEMIC FREEDOM

28-1. In our representative democracy, in which ultimate power is retained by the people and exercised through delegation of authority, the Board and the Association advocate the realization of the full potential of each individual by recognition of and respect for his-her dignity. It therefore follows that the education of each individual must develop the essential fundamental processes and those skills, understandings, and attitudes which will affect his-her harmonious development as a spiritual, intellectual, physical, emotional, and social being. It is recognized that these democratic values can best be transmitted in an atmosphere which is free from censorship and artificial restraints upon free inquiry and learning, and in which academic freedom for teacher and student is encouraged.

28-2. category_summaries.summary: The Jersey City Board of Education recognizes the Jersey City Education Association (JCEA) as the exclusive and sole bargaining representative and exclusive representative for professional negotiations, with recognition not impairing any employee’s rights. “Employee” includes all members of the bargaining unit, and any negotiated agreement applies to all teachers. The parties pledge that their representatives have necessary authority to make and consider proposals and counter-proposals. The contract also provides for JCEA recognition-related administration, including the Board’s obligation to deduct JCEA membership dues from authorized employees’ salaries (until termination/cessation), with the JCEA certifying the current annual dues amount and the Board providing and updating monthly lists of voluntarily authorized employees; teachers may revoke authorization by notifying the Board and the Association. Additionally, the Association’s representatives and rights under the agreement are limited to the JCEA, and the Association has at least three (3) voting members appointed to the Board of Personnel Practices by the Association President, while the superintendent appoints teachers selected by the Association.

The agreement is effective as of September 1, 1978 and remains in full force and effect until August 31, 1980, with the parties’ right to negotiate modifications. The parties also agree to enter into good-faith negotiations for a successor agreement, beginning no later than October 3 of the school year in which the current agreement expires, with the understanding that any necessary extension of the negotiation/period must be by mutual agreement between the Superintendent’s Office and the Association. A successor agreement must be reduced to writing, signed by the Board and the Association, and submitted to the Board for adoption; it may not be modified in whole or in part except by a written instrument duly executed by both parties. Neither party is required to negotiate any subject unless mutually agreed. Any authorization relating to continuation/termination is terminable only by prior written notice effective January 1 or July 1 of any year, and the committee is to submit a written report with recommendations within the 1978–80 school years; the parties must also exchange copies of current agreements and, where applicable, supplements and updated expiration dates.

The Board retains and reserves all governance powers and may adopt policies, rules, and practices to carry them out, but such exercise is limited only by the Agreement’s terms. Within that framework, teachers maintain key instructional and classroom authority: they determine grades; they have authority in the classroom and primary disciplinary responsibility; they may recommend suspension of pupils and may send students to the principal; and teachers must plan their work and provide plans for supervisory visitation. Administrators and supervisors are responsible to support teachers in disciplinary roles. Board appointment governs the filling of the listed administrative and supervisory positions, while the Superintendent assigns newly appointed personnel to specific subject areas and/or grade levels; teachers cannot be assigned outside the scope of their teaching certificates and/or major/minor fields of study (except where an emergency exists). In emergencies, an Association Building Director may request the immediate supervisor to temporarily relieve the building director. The Board selects personnel for various roles (including specialists) based on published criteria and final Board choice where multiple candidates express interest; it will employ during the Agreement at least nineteen (19) specialists and additional specialists and additional bilingual teachers, and it will hire only fully certified teachers to the fullest extent possible. The Board continues moving toward class-size reduction through increased physical facilities, and multi-media materials must be arranged to maximize utility by the instructional staff under the principal’s auspices.

Compensation provisions include that Association representatives performing duties under the agreement shall suffer no loss of pay, and affected teachers receive compensation on a schedule of two (2) salary checks per month for twelve (12) months, paid on the 1st and 16th (or the last prior school day if those dates fall on a weekend/non-school day), with summer payments requiring completed self-addressed envelopes for mailing. Deductions for teacher absences when schools are in session less than the customary 5½ hours are calculated based on actual hours lost, with the day-school per diem not forfeited; salary deductions use one-half (1/2) substitute per diem pay. Extra-compensation positions include those in Schedule H, and substitute teacher per diem salary is $35.00. Summer school teaching is paid at $9 per hour. Teachers resigning after ten (10) years of regularly appointed service or upon retirement receive a lump-sum payment. National Guard and Naval Militia employees receive the difference between their pay and military pay. Salary advancement provisions include that teachers appointed on/after September 1, 1963 must hold a Master’s degree for advanced salary standing, and the equivalency program phase applies only to teachers appointed prior to that date; incremental increases are provided, and salaries may be increased above Schedule A for prior satisfactory certified teaching experience. Longevity/extended service payments include $500 upon completion of 16 years and another $500 upon completion of 25 years (in addition to the scheduled salary guide), plus varsity/junior varsity increases of $100 per person and male athletic coaches receiving extended-service increments of $100 after 5 years, a second $100 after 10 years, and a third $100 after 20 years.

Scheduling provisions provide for teachers to receive their preparation periods and, where possible, uninterrupted daily preparation time; however, the entire school system is limited to no more than fifteen (15) additional preparation periods per week for such purposes, and the use of a regular teacher as a substitute to deprive them of preparation is prohibited except in emergencies when regular substitutes are unavailable. Assignments must generally be issued at least three (3) days before school closes, and teachers affected by changes are to be notified promptly in writing (including new teachers, for whom notice must be given as early as possible but no later than August 22). Teacher schedules for assignments across multiple schools must minimize inter-school travel. Principals (or authorized personnel) must notify faculty of required meetings at least two (2) days in advance. Staffing and scheduling also address equitable coverage in emergencies, including calling teachers to cover classes from a rotating list; regular teachers are to be assigned first on a voluntary basis during non-teaching time before rotating assignments, and secondary teachers are limited to no more than two (2) subject-matter teaching preparations per day. Normal high school scheduling includes five (5) teaching periods, a home room, and a special assignment, with specified equivalency for home room duty (one-half of a study, assigned-duty, or recitation period), and teachers normally teaching no more than two periods consecutively; in double-period subjects (e.g., Physical Education, Industrial Arts), variation from the normal schedule is permitted. The in-school work day is capped at not more than five (5) hours and forty-five (45) minutes, with duty-free lunch minimums of at least forty-five (45) minutes in high schools, at least sixty (60) minutes in elementary schools, and one-half hour for Special Education classes (supported by employing lunchroom aides), and Elementary coaching teachers are to receive an unassigned period at the end of the school day where feasible. Additional scheduling/operations items include textbooks ordered for an August 15 delivery, limits on teacher workdays (no more than 180 days per school year), teacher reporting/leave time and pupil reporting times (teachers 8:30 A.M.; pupils 10:00 A.M.), receipt of checks prior to A.M. dismissal, time for faculty services/parent meetings as requested, the priority of efficient utilization of school facilities/personnel, making snow/other emergency closings up during the spring, and following State guidelines for Special Education and kindergarten so they are not used in computing median class size (with the desirable median class size set at 30 pupils, exclusive of health and physical education).

The agreement provides that teachers receive and accrue sick leave, including fourteen (14) accumulative sick leave days annually, with one (1) additional day for each year of service upon the Superintendent’s recommendation and the Medical Director’s approval, and it adds days to the sick leave bank (including one additional day for teachers). Teachers are entitled to full salary and other benefits for absences due to personal illness in accordance with permitted leave, and they do not forfeit accumulated sick or personal leave for such qualifying absences. If a teacher does not use all permissive leave in a school year, unused days may be requested in writing to be applied within the same school year (to June 30) to new illness leave. For absences beyond accumulated personal illness/permissive personal illness leave, the teacher may be allowed up to forty (40) days (or up to eighty (80) days if applicable) in a school year, but for those additional periods the teacher forfeits one-half (1/2) of the substitute per diem pay; salary payment is discontinued for further absence. Sick leave bank payouts include an option to trade one-half (1/2) of accumulated Jersey City sick days after September 1, 1972, and an estate lump sum payment upon death before retirement. Teachers may be excused without loss of pay or accumulated leave for up to five (5) consecutive calendar days (e.g., funeral day excusals without loss), certain faculty religious services attendance, up to three (3) days per year for religious observance, absences due to quarantine by the Board of Health without pay deductions, and absences for subpoena/summons without pay deductions, with notice requirements to the principal (including expected return dates and probable illness duration). For absences of five (5) days or less, a personal certificate must be filed upon return; teachers absent two (2) days or more must notify the principal by the prior school day. Maternity leave requires pregnant married women to apply at least three (3) months before expected birth, with eligibility thirty (30) days later for maternity leave without pay for two (2) calendar years plus additional time through the following August 31, and further maternity leave is permitted in limited circumstances (including one additional leave for later pregnancy during an existing leave). Adoption leaves are eligible for similar leave to maternity. For non-regular teachers who become pregnant, services end forty-five (45) days after written notice to the Superintendent (at least three (3) months before expected birth), with return subject to Medical Director approval and further unpaid leave (up to one (1) year) possible until recovery. Teachers on study or rest and recuperation leave receive salary compensation of one-half (1/2) monthly salary for each month of such twelve (12)-month (beginning September 1) leave, may request cancellation, must apply in advance (three (3) months for rest/recuperation; four (4) months for study), and are restricted from remunerative work during the leave (excluding certain scholarships/grants/stipends). Personal business leave may be granted by the Board for up to one (1) year with loss of pay, except teachers are entitled to two (2) personal business days per year without loss of pay, and unused personal business days are transferred to the sick leave bank; requests must generally reach the Superintendent’s office three (3) days prior to the day of leave unless waived. Military leave is addressed by providing military leave without pay for service periods and, for pay differences, providing the difference between teacher pay and military pay, with additional periods granted without pay. Additional protected leave includes allowing professional staff to attend one professional meeting annually outside Jersey City without loss of pay, with requests made three (3) days in advance.

The Board of Education must make available to teachers individual health insurance under the New Jersey Public and School Employees Health Benefits Plan, including Rider “J,” and provide the health-care insurance protection described in master policies and contracts agreed upon by the Board and the Association. The Board pays the full premium for each teacher and, for teachers employed for the full school year, makes premium payments to cover the twelve-month period from September 1 through August 31, with retroactive or prospective premium adjustments as needed to ensure uninterrupted coverage. In addition, the Board provides an individual dental plan and an individual prescription plan, and supplies each teacher with a written description of the coverage. The Board also provides life insurance of $2,500 and death and dismemberment insurance of $2,500 per teacher; upon retirement, life coverage reduces to $1,000 and the death and dismemberment coverage is cancelled, with the $1,000 post-retirement life premium paid by the retiree.

Under the Ancillary-related provisions, a teacher is eligible to receive benefits described in sections 32-3 and 32-4 only if the teacher satisfies the requirements set out in section 32-2. Additionally, upon completing 30 years of service in the Jersey City School System, the teacher becomes entitled to a $500 benefit.

Security-related provisions require that teachers may not be disciplined, reprimanded, reduced in rank/compensation, or deprived of professional advantages without just cause, and that teachers be properly notified of their status for the ensuing school year (by April 1 for contract teachers; by April 30 for non-tenured, regularly appointed teachers). Teachers’ contract status for the ensuing year cannot be denied except for cause, and teachers are not to be routinely assigned outside the scope of their teaching certificates. For filling extra-compensation and other Board-established positions, vacancies must be publicly posted in all schools within specified short timeframes after the vacancy/new position occurs (e.g., seven (7) school days, and in some cases five (5) school days), with notices stating duties, requirements, and qualifications. Selection is guided by preferences such as qualified applicants currently employed by the Board and, for Accredited Evening High School positions, preference based on prior teaching experience there; additional assignments are made from written application lists. Promotions/extra-compensation applied for are treated as voluntary transfers. Transfers are governed by written requests submitted by March 1, specified content (reasons and requested schools/grades/subjects, with up to three choices), a cap of transfers not exceeding 5% of the staff in the sending school, and allocation principles such as honoring convenience/wishes unless conflicting with instructional needs; seniority rules differ for voluntary (starts upon assuming the new position) versus involuntary transfers (accrued seniority retained). Temporary filling of vacancies is permitted, but only true vacancies (e.g., new positions, resignation, retirement, termination, death) may be filled by transfers. Coaching re-employment is handled through notification (no annual application required; notification within sixty (60) days after the season), with vacancy handling focused on assistant coaches and published/eligibility procedures (e.g., fifteen (15) days to indicate interest; eligibility criteria of five (5) years experience or Physical Education Department membership), while keeping the number of specialists/substitutes at agreed minimums (substitutes not less than forty (40)).

Training and professional development provisions include examination requirements and continuing-skill support: no candidate may take the oral portion of an examination unless the written portion has been passed. Examinations consist of a written section weighted at 40% and an oral interview weighted at 60%, conducted by a Board of Personnel Practices that must include professional educators not regularly employed by the Board of Education. For approved study, the nature and scope of the program must be approved by the Superintendent of Schools. To encourage the Professional Staff in the Jersey City Public Schools to improve professional skills, the Board agrees to provide in-service courses each year, with a five-member course/selection body composed of three members named by the Association and two named by the Board. The Board will also consider providing behind-the-wheel instruction. Additionally, teaching staff with at least seven (7) years of continuous and satisfactory public-school service in Jersey City are referenced in the staff qualification context, and teachers appointed on or after September 1, 1963 must have a Master’s Degree to be eligible for advanced salary standing.

The parties agree to resolve disputes through good-faith negotiations and a structured grievance procedure covering salaries, terms and conditions of employment, and matters adversely affecting working conditions or welfare, with employees assured freedom from restraint, interference, coercion, discrimination, or reprisal and the right to present grievances (including representation by Association-approved representatives). Employees must first orally advise the principal, who must meet within three (3) school days and communicate an oral decision within three (3) school days after the discussion; if not resolved, the grievance may be presented within five (5) calendar days to the JCEA Grievance Evaluation Team, which must decide within seven (7) calendar days and notify the involved person in writing. The grieving party may submit written statements and, at the applicable step, be accompanied by up to two (2) Association representatives designated by the Team; the principal must hold meetings on request and issue written decisions within five (5) school days, with copies to the Superintendent. Appeals may be made to the Superintendent within ten (10) calendar days (with documents attached) and the Superintendent must decide within six (6) school days; if unresolved at Step III, the employee may request Board of Education review within seven (7) school days, in writing through the Superintendent (who attaches and forwards all related documents). An employee must institute action within fifteen (15) school days after the occurrence complained of (or, for grievances tied to the annual statement items, within fifteen (15) months after receipt of that statement). If decisions are not issued within prescribed time limits, the grievant may proceed to the next step on notice, and any time limits may be extended by mutual agreement; no loss of pay results from pursuing the procedure, and employees may proceed directly to Step III in certain circumstances (e.g., where the GET contends there is merit). If still unresolved, the grievant may request arbitration—made no later than fifteen (15) school days after disposition at Step IV—where the arbitrator’s decision is final and binding on both parties, but the arbitrator cannot alter the Agreement’s terms or issue decisions requiring an unlawful act or violating the Agreement. Arbitration costs for abatement are paid by the unsuccessful party, all meetings/hearings are private (not public) and limited to parties in interest and designated representatives, and either party may have recourse, including circumstances where group/class grievances may be submitted directly to the Superintendent.

The agreement provides for multiple safety-related measures, including safe storage for teachers’ personal possessions; furnishing each teacher with a serviceable desk and chair; and ensuring sufficient instructional materials are available upon timely request (except emergencies). Teachers are not required to work under unsafe or hazardous conditions, and any unsafe conditions must be reported immediately to the principal or responsible authority for correction. To address student and workplace safety, the Board and Association will develop mutually acceptable programs to guarantee safety of students, teachers, and property, and will establish committees and facilities/resources as needed, including reading labs in three (3) schools, use of at least two driving simulators in existing driver education courses, and equipment for pupil services (ten (10) tape recorders and ten (10) dictaphones). The contract also includes anti-assault protections: the Board will provide legal services and furnish legal counsel for proceedings arising from assaults on teachers during employment; teachers must immediately report any physical or verbal assault to their principal or immediate superior; teachers may use reasonable and necessary force within the scope of employment for self-defense and for protection of persons or property; and the Board will reimburse the reasonable cost of clothing or other personal property damaged or destroyed as a result of an assault suffered by a teacher. Additional practical protections include requiring non-tenured teachers to submit lesson-plan books and all teachers to have emergency lesson plans to guide substitute teachers.

The Agreement includes various miscellaneous provisions: the Board will not negotiate with any organization other than the Association regarding unit employees for the Agreement’s duration, and both parties will act in good faith to carry out the Agreement. It bars the Board from being required to honor certain authorizations for deductions and protects teachers’ rights to wear Association membership identification. The Association may distribute materials via teachers’ mailboxes (with the principal/designee notified in advance), and Association representatives (including JCEA/NJEA/NEA and the JCEA President/designee) may enter schools to meet teachers, provided required advance notice to the principal/designee is given and, for the 1st Vice President, time for Association business is limited to not more than two and one-half (2.5) days per full week and must not disrupt education. The Association receives exclusive system-wide bargaining-agent bulletin boards (acceptable existing boards in good condition; no access to other organizations’ bulletin/display/mail space), and may use school buildings at reasonable hours subject to usual Board procedures. Miscellaneous operational provisions include access to a public pay telephone for exclusive teacher use; teacher personnel file inspection rights upon advance written request, with written comments (after review by the Assistant Superintendent for Personnel) becoming part of the file; and rules relating to transfer of books between schools. The Board establishes petty cash funds at each school each year in specified amounts (by school-year provision). Joint/standing committees are continued or created, including: a joint committee to study an aide program; liaisons among teacher, police, and courts in appropriate ways; committees on athletics (at least three (3) meetings per year with Association representatives), award systems, and a continued joint BREAKFAST COMMITTEE with periodic reports to the Board; and committees to develop federal-funded projects and advise on textbook/curriculum matters (with specified membership composition). The Agreement also provides for Board reimbursement of teachers’ defense costs in proceedings arising from duties, ongoing evaluation/establishment of awards and parking-facility recommendations by designated committee members, and protection against reprisals of any kind against teachers/JCEA members. Additional provisions include provisions on: publishing summer school openings and reporting teacher applications to the Board; limiting applicants’ written commitments not to accept another administrator/supervisor/teacher position during a specified period; providing one (1) mobil learning center for the Agreement’s life; continuing to evaluate school facilities and emergency school building aid; expanding central registers by adding one (1) to existing registers during each of the two agreement years; and Association-led contract printing, with the Association preparing the contract form and printer submissions, and both parties paying one-half of the final printing costs for 4,000 booklet copies. Administrative/board-rule conflicts are to be modified to conform to collective-bargaining agreements, and examples of miscellaneous administrative items include the Agreement form/record openness to use and specific closing date language (School Closes—Wednesday, June 25, 1980).
